issues.subcategory: Discussion contradicts Results (anxiety effect)
issues.description: The Discussion repeatedly claims that the high-risk period before attempts was associated with greater anxiety, but Primary Analysis 1 found no significant effect of episode type on anxiety (χ²(3)=3.62, p=.306 in Table 2). Only sad words reached significance, and that effect was not unique to attempts. Asserting an anxiety mean difference that the data do not support misrepresents the findings.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.subcategory: Sign error in iatrogenic table vs text
issues.description: The Results text states desire to die significantly decreased from pre (M=0.82) to post (M=0.61), a change of about -0.21. However, Table 1 reports the pre-to-post change in desire to die as +0.20 (an increase). The two directly contradict each other on the direction of the effect, undermining confidence in the safety/iatrogenic reporting.
issues.quote: Desire to die (0-10) | 0.20

issues.subcategory: Contradictory counts of attempters with SMS data
issues.description: The manuscript states that of 27 participants with SMS data, only 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt. Yet it later states that 13 participants reported a single attempt and 14 reported multiple attempts (13+14=27) 'among attempters with SMS data.' These figures cannot both be correct and make it unclear how many participants actually contributed attempt-episode data to the key analyses.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.

issues.subcategory: Underpowered key comparison / unbalanced contributors
issues.description: The central within-subjects comparisons hinge on attempt episodes, but only ~15 participants (and 21 attempt episodes) contributed attempt data, while 12 participants contributed no attempt data at all yet were retained. Effects described as 'unique to attempts' therefore rest on a very small subset, and the between-episode contrasts are based on different, partly non-overlapping sets of participants, threatening the validity of within-subject inference.
issues.quote: the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses

issues.subcategory: Power-analysis numbers inconsistent with actual sample
issues.description: The a priori power analysis assumes 30 attempters representing 60 attempts with only 20 usable SMS attempts, but the realized sample was 33 participants of whom only ~15 had attempt SMS data and 21 attempts with SMS data. The discrepancy between the planning assumptions and the achieved data is not reconciled, making the stated power claims difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes

issues.subcategory: Retrospective design mislabeled as prospective
issues.description: Reconstructing past episodes from a retrospective clinical interview is a retrospective design. Labeling it 'a prospective research design' is conceptually incorrect and conflates the directionality of the language data (collected before episodes) with the directionality of the study design (episodes identified after the fact). This mislabeling overstates the inferential strength of the design.
issues.quote: we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a ‘true’ prospective study design

issues.subcategory: Predictive/real-time claims from retrospective correlational data
issues.description: The title and conclusions frame the work as identifying suicide risk 'in real time' and as identifying 'novel predictors of suicidal behaviors,' but the data are retrospective, correlational, and episodes were classified after the fact. No prospective prediction was tested. These framing choices overstate causal and predictive validity.
issues.quote: This laboratory investigation identified novel predictors of suicidal behaviors, which may be utilized in the future by machine learning models to predict acute suicide risk

issues.subcategory: Multiple comparisons uncorrected with many marginal p-values
issues.description: A large number of mixed-effects models and pairwise tests were run, and most 'significant' findings are barely below .05 (e.g., p=.049, .046, .033, .035, .024). The authors explicitly chose not to correct for multiple comparisons. Given the number of tests and the marginal p-values, several key findings would not survive correction, inflating the likelihood of false positives.
issues.quote: we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats

issues.subcategory: Data-driven selection of time window
issues.description: Although the two-week window is described as set a priori 'conservatively,' the authors also report empirically inspecting loess-smoothed figures to identify where change was most pronounced (around 7 days). Using the observed data to inform the analysis window is a researcher degree of freedom that can bias results, and it is not clear whether any analysis decisions followed from this inspection.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of likelihood-ratio and Wald tests
issues.description: The manuscript labels the model-comparison tests as 'Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests,' but likelihood-ratio tests and Wald chi-square tests are distinct procedures with different statistics and assumptions. This conflation creates ambiguity about which test was actually performed to evaluate the fixed effects reported in Tables 2 and 3.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.subcategory: Effect size magnitude mislabeled
issues.description: The power analysis describes Cramer's V = 0.29 as the threshold for detecting 'only large effect sizes.' By conventional benchmarks, V≈0.3 corresponds to a medium effect, not a large one. Mislabeling the detectable effect size leads to an overly optimistic characterization of the study's sensitivity.
issues.quote: would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models

issues.subcategory: Broad 'suicide attempt' definition lacking physical harm
issues.description: The operationalization of 'suicide attempt' includes aborted/interrupted incidents in which no action was taken (71% involved no physical harm, and some were classified by participants' subjective endorsement only). This substantially broadens the construct and means the 'high-risk attempt' category is heterogeneous and may not reflect actual suicide attempts, weakening the validity of the central contrast.
issues.quote: 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm (e.g., driving to high place, such as a bridge, but deciding not to jump)

issues.subcategory: Large, potentially non-random episode-level missingness
issues.description: Only 134 of 293 episodes (46%) had SMS data, and iPhone encryption selectively blocked extraction for some users. The mixed-model justification assumes data are missing at random, but more recent episodes and certain device/user types are more likely to have data, making missingness plausibly non-random. This is not addressed and could bias episode comparisons.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data

issues.subcategory: Narrow sample extrapolated to clinical monitoring and suicide deaths
issues.description: The sample is overwhelmingly young (M=20.4), female (84.8%), White college students who made largely non-injurious attempts, yet the Discussion extrapolates to objective real-time monitoring tools, suicide completers, and broad public-health applications. The mismatch between the sample and the populations of ultimate interest (e.g., males, who die by suicide ~4x more often) is acknowledged only partially while strong generalizing claims persist.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals’ communication “behind the scenes,”

issues.subcategory: Implausible variance-explained claim
issues.description: The claim that a risk model 'accounted for 80.3% of the variance' for suicide attempts is implausible for a rare outcome and conflicts with the paper's own thesis that suicide risk prediction is poor. This figure is likely a misreporting of a different metric (e.g., classification/discrimination), and presenting it as variance explained misleads the reader about the state of the field.
issues.quote: a recent model, which included known risk factors for suicide attempt, accounted for 80.3% of the variance (Nock, Borges, & Ono, 2012)

issues.subcategory: Undefined time anchor (day 0) for non-attempt episodes
issues.description: The slope analyses align all episode types on a -14 to 0 day axis, with day 0 being the attempt for attempt episodes. It is never specified what day 0 represents for ideation, depressed, and positive episodes (which have 'no theoretical expectation of temporal change'). Without a meaningful anchor for the comparison episodes, the interaction (slope difference) tests are difficult to interpret or replicate.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0), and the interaction of episode type and day

issues.subcategory: No blinding of interviewer who classified episodes
issues.description: The same experimenter conducted recruitment, the interview, and the classification of episodes into risk categories, which also anchored the outcome analyses. There is no mention of blinding or independent classification, raising the possibility that knowledge of hypotheses influenced episode dating and categorization—particularly important given the reliance on subjective, single-informant report.
issues.quote: participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes, including dates of past suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: Marginal effects overinterpreted as 'unique'
issues.description: Effects described as 'unique to attempts' rest on barely-significant uncorrected pairwise contrasts (e.g., positive emotion attempt vs. ideation z=1.96, p=.049; anger attempt vs. ideation z=2.00, p=.046). Characterizing these as robust, attempt-specific signals overstates the strength and specificity of the evidence given the marginal values and number of tests.
issues.quote: Unique to attempts, positive emotion decreased and anger increased to a greater extent as one approached a suicide attempt, relative to the other episode types.

issues.subcategory: Social engagement operationalized too coarsely
issues.description: Perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness (interpersonal theory constructs) are operationalized only as counts/ratios of sent vs. received messages. These aggregate metrics do not capture the theoretical constructs (who initiates, unanswered messages, content of rejection), so a null result cannot be interpreted as evidence against the theory. The authors note this only after presenting it as a test of the hypothesis.
issues.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages

issues.subcategory: Missing scale anchors and effect-size estimates
issues.description: Key descriptive ratings (e.g., intent M=3.95, lethality M=3.38) are reported without specifying the response scale range or anchors, preventing evaluation of whether intent/lethality were truly 'high.' Additionally, the inferential models report log-odds betas as effect sizes without confidence intervals, limiting interpretability and replicability.
issues.quote: participants reported fairly high intent to kill themselves (M=3.95, SD=0.86) and subjective judgment of the lethality of the suicide method was reasonably high (M=3.38, SD=0.86)

issues.subcategory: CONSORT diagram for non-randomized observational study
issues.description: A CONSORT flow diagram is referenced, but CONSORT is designed for randomized controlled trials. Using it here may misrepresent the study type and does not substitute for a clear account of how observational participants and episodes were retained or excluded at each stage, including the device-related data losses.
issues.quote: See Figure S1 (in the Supplemental Material available online) for a CONSORT diagram detailing specific numbers and reasons for exclusion.
